screens.title: Advertising Routes into BGP
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we'll learn the concrete rules and best practices for injecting routes into BGP on Junos devices. You will learn three primary methods: the network statement for advertising locally originated prefixes, redistribution of routes learned by other protocols through explicit routing policies, and aggregation or summary approaches. We'll also cover a vital operational detail: BGP address families — specifically family inet unicast — and why forgetting it prevents IPv4 routes from being exchanged. Throughout the lesson you'll see exact Junos configuration examples, verification commands to confirm what your router is advertising and receiving, and a short lab scenario to practice advertising a static prefix and redistributing OSPF routes. These skills matter because BGP will not advertise routes by default; explicit, precise configuration decides what your AS tells peers about reachability. By the end you will be able to ensure a prefix exists in the routing table before advertising it, craft export policies that only allow intended routes, and verify the results with show route advertising-protocol and receive-protocol queries. Keep an eye out for common pitfalls like missing family statements or overly-broad redistribution policies that can cause accidental leakage of internal routes.

screens.title: The network statement — exact-match advertising
screens.narratorSegment: The network statement is the simplest and most explicit way to tell Junos BGP to advertise a prefix. The key detail is that the network command does not create a route; it only instructs BGP to advertise a prefix if an exact match for that prefix and mask exists in the router's inet.0 table. Practically, this means operators often add a static route with next-hop discard or a connected interface to guarantee the prefix is present. For example, configuring a static route to 172.16.1.0/24 with next-hop discard ensures the prefix is active, then setting network 172.16.1.0/24 under the BGP group causes the router to announce it. A common misconception is that the network statement alone will create reachability; it will not. Another pitfall is using a wrong mask — an exact-match requirement will silently prevent advertisement. Use show route to confirm the prefix is in inet.0 before expecting it to be advertised. The concrete takeaway is: network adds the advertisement only if the router already knows how to reach that prefix. Test this in the lab by adding and removing the static route and observing advertising-protocol output.

keyIdea.title: Network statement rule
keyIdea.text: A network statement advertises only exact-match prefixes that exist in the inet.0 routing table; it does not create reachability.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.5 › Network statement
Definition

Network statement

Instructs BGP to advertise a specific prefix only when that exact prefix exists in inet.0. It will not create routes.

Why it matters
  • Prevents advertising unreachable prefixes.
  • Clear operational intent: advertise only known prefixes.
  • Works well with a static discard route or connected summary.
Common misconception

Some expect network to add the route automatically; it does not. Always verify the route is in inet.0.

Configuration example
set routing-options static route 172.16.1.0/24 next-hop discard
set protocols bgp group EBGP_PEER family inet unicast
set protocols bgp group EBGP_PEER neighbor 10.0.0.2 peer-as 65002
set protocols bgp group EBGP_PEER network 172.16.1.0/24
Example
Add static discard so the network statement has a route to advertise.
Check
Use show route 172.16.1.0/24 and show route advertising-protocol bgp 10.0.0.2
Key Takeaway

Network statements require an exact-match route in the local routing table; configure reachability or a discard route first.

screens.title: Ensure route existence before advertising
screens.narratorSegment: Before BGP can advertise a prefix via a network statement, that prefix must be present and active in the inet.0 routing table. There are three common ways to ensure existence: a directly connected interface, a static route, or an aggregate/summary created by static or OSPF configuration. A widely used operational pattern is to add a static route with next-hop discard for summary or non-connected networks. This creates a stable route in inet.0 without pointing traffic into a black hole, and it lets BGP advertise the prefix. Another option is to use an aggregate or summary advertisement if you want to represent many specific prefixes as a single larger prefix — but be careful because summarization changes what you advertise to peers. A practical lab exercise: configure a static discard for 192.168.50.0/24, confirm show route 192.168.50.0/24 returns an active route, then add the network statement. If the route disappears from inet.0 later, BGP will stop advertising it. A common troubleshooting step is to check for more specific routes or route preferences that might suppress the static route from becoming active. Ensure route existence before advertising means guarantee the advertised prefix exists in inet.0 using static, connected, or aggregate routes so bgp will advertise it.. In practical terms, how to make a prefix present in inet.0 so the network statement takes effect. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.5 › Ensure route existence
Process

Make the prefix present

  1. Add a static route with next-hop discard for summaries or non-connected networks.
  2. Or configure the interface with the specific address so the prefix is directly connected.
  3. Or create an aggregate summary route if appropriate for your routing design.
Troubleshooting tips
  • Check for more specific routes that override a static entry.
  • Verify the static route is active with show route.
  • Remember BGP will stop advertising if the route is removed from inet.0.
Example configuration
set routing-options static route 192.168.50.0/24 next-hop discard
set protocols bgp group EBGP_PEER family inet unicast
set protocols bgp group EBGP_PEER network 192.168.50.0/24
Verify
show route 192.168.50.0/24 then show route advertising-protocol bgp 10.0.0.2
Caution
If another route is preferred, the static discard may be inactive. Check route preference and protocols.
Key Takeaway

Create an explicit route in inet.0 before relying on a network statement to advertise it.

screens.title: family inet unicast — address-family essentials
screens.narratorSegment: BGP is multi-protocol by design: it carries routes for different address families such as IPv4 unicast, IPv6 unicast, and various VPN families. On Junos, each BGP group must explicitly enable the address family you want to exchange. For standard IPv4 routing you must include family inet unicast under the BGP group. If you configure network statements or export policies but forget family inet unicast, the router will not advertise or accept IPv4 unicast routes for that neighbor. This is a common operational mistake and one of the easiest to overlook during peer configuration. In practice, add family inet unicast to every eBGP or iBGP group that will carry IPv4. After enabling, verify peers exchange routes using show route protocol bgp and the advertising/receive-protocol commands. Remember that enabling a family does not itself permit every route — it only allows the exchange of that family subject to your network statements and export policies. A brief misconception check: some operators assume family is global; on Junos it is per-group and must be set per peering relationship. family inet unicast — address-family essentials means family inet unicast must be configured on the bgp group to exchange ipv4 unicast routes; forgetting it prevents ipv4 advertisements.. In practical terms, why you must enable ipv4 unicast on each bgp group. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Family enabler
keyIdea.text: family inet unicast must be configured on the BGP group to exchange IPv4 unicast routes; forgetting it prevents IPv4 advertisements.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.5 › family inet unicast
Definition

Address-family requirement

Enable family inet unicast under the BGP group to permit IPv4 unicast route exchange with that neighbor.

Operational note

This is a per-group setting on Junos. Forgetting to set it is a common reason why IPv4 routes are not advertised, even with correctly configured network statements and policies.

Misconception

Some expect BGP to enable families globally; on Junos it is explicit per group.

Example snippet
set protocols bgp group EBGP_PEER type external
set protocols bgp group EBGP_PEER neighbor 10.0.0.2 peer-as 65002
set protocols bgp group EBGP_PEER family inet unicast
Verification

After enabling family inet unicast, confirm routes with show route protocol bgp and show route advertising-protocol bgp <neighbor> to ensure IPv4 prefixes are exchanged.

Key Takeaway

Explicitly enable the address family for the type of routes you expect to exchange; family inet unicast is required for IPv4.

screens.title: Redistribution into BGP using routing policies
screens.narratorSegment: Redistribution into BGP on Junos is not an implicit action; it is performed by attaching an export policy to a BGP group. Routing policies are the central control point — they let you match routes by protocol, prefix, or route-filter and then accept, reject, or modify attributes before export. A common pattern is to write a policy that matches protocol ospf and accept only those routes you intend to advertise, then attach that policy to the BGP group's export statement. This gives precise control and reduces accidental leaks. For example you can match protocol ospf and then add an additional from route-filter to limit to certain prefixes. A frequent operator error is to write a policy that never matches or to forget that policy-statements have an implicit deny at the end. Always test policies with test policy before applying them to a live BGP session. The architecture pattern here is simple: routing protocols feed the routing table, policies select and manipulate candidates, and BGP exports validated prefixes to peers. The safety and traceability provided by policies are why redistribution on Junos is policy-driven rather than automatic.

keyIdea.title: Policy-driven redistribution
keyIdea.text: Routing policies decide which non-BGP routes are exported; attach an export policy to the BGP group to control redistribution.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.5 › Redistribution via policies
Architecture

Routing policies control redistribution

Policies let you filter and accept routes from OSPF, static, or direct protocols before exporting them into BGP. They provide safety and precision.

Rules of thumb
  • Match by protocol or route-filter to narrow candidates.
  • Test policies with test policy against sample prefixes.
  • Remember implicit deny at policy end — add explicit accept terms.
Example policy and application
set policy-options policy-statement REDISTRIBUTE_OSPF_TO_BGP term OSPF_ROUTES from protocol ospf
set policy-options policy-statement REDISTRIBUTE_OSPF_TO_BGP term OSPF_ROUTES then accept
set protocols bgp group EBGP_PEER export REDISTRIBUTE_OSPF_TO_BGP
Pro tip
Add route-filter or prefix-list clauses to limit which OSPF routes are exported.
Common mistake
Applying a broad policy that accepts all direct or OSPF routes can leak internal prefixes to the internet.
Key Takeaway

Always use routing policies to control redistribution; test them before applying as export to a BGP group.

screens.title: Creating and testing an export policy
screens.narratorSegment: When you create an export policy to redistribute OSPF routes into BGP, follow a clear process: define the policy with specific match conditions, test it using test policy, then attach it to the BGP group's export statement. Begin by writing a policy-statement with a term that matches protocol ospf. If you need narrower control, add a from route-filter clause for the desired prefixes. After you write the policy, use show policy policy-statement detail to inspect its terms, and use test policy to simulate how the policy would act on a sample route. Testing prevents surprises and the common error of implicit deny. Once verified, apply the policy to the BGP group with set protocols bgp group export. After applying, verify with show route advertising-protocol bgp to see the actual exported prefixes. The concrete example in the chapter shows a policy called REDISTRIBUTE_OSPF_TO_BGP and the exact configuration lines to create and apply it. Remember: testing before applying to live peers reduces risk. Creating and testing an export policy means always test your policy with test policy and inspect with show policy before applying it to bgp to avoid an implicit deny or unintended accepts.. In practical terms, write a policy that matches ospf routes and test it before export. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Always test your policy with test policy and inspect with show policy before applying it to BGP to avoid an implicit deny or unintended accepts.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.5 › Export policy walkthrough
Steps
  1. Create a policy-statement matching protocol ospf and any prefix filters you need.
  2. Test the policy with test policy <name> <sample-route> to confirm behavior.
  3. Apply the policy to the BGP group using export <policy-name>.
  4. Verify advertised routes with show route advertising-protocol bgp <neighbor>.
Why test?

Testing avoids unintentionally accepting nothing due to an implicit deny or accepting too many prefixes because of a loose filter.

Example commands
set policy-options policy-statement REDISTRIBUTE_OSPF_TO_BGP term 1 from protocol ospf
set policy-options policy-statement REDISTRIBUTE_OSPF_TO_BGP term 1 then accept
# Test with
run show configuration policy-options policy-statement REDISTRIBUTE_OSPF_TO_BGP
run test policy REDISTRIBUTE_OSPF_TO_BGP route 10.10.10.1/32
# Apply to BGP
set protocols bgp group EBGP_PEER export REDISTRIBUTE_OSPF_TO_BGP
Verification
show route advertising-protocol bgp 10.0.0.2 to confirm exported prefixes.
Pitfall
Do not skip test policy; an untested policy can block all routes due to implicit deny.

screens.title: Network statement vs Redistribution
screens.narratorSegment: Choose the network statement when you want to advertise a small set of locally originated prefixes that you can make present in inet.0. It is simple and explicit: the network statement advertises an exact prefix only if that prefix exists. Use it for static summaries, loopbacks, or a handful of important prefixes. Use redistribution with routing policies when you need to export routes learned from other protocols, for example many OSPF-learned internal routes or specific static entries. Redistribution gives granular control: you can select protocols and apply route-filters, set attributes, and avoid leaking internal topology. A common operational decision is to use network statements for static and summary prefixes where reachability is controlled, and use carefully crafted export policies for redistributing large sets of protocol-learned routes. The key trade-off is simplicity versus scale and control. Network statements are straightforward but require the route to exist; policies are more flexible but require careful testing to prevent over-advertising. Consider the size of what you must export and the safety required when deciding between the two. Network statement vs Redistribution means network is simple and exact-match; redistribution via policies is flexible and scalable but requires testing and filtering.. In practical terms, when to use network statements and when to use policy-based redistribution. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Common mistakes and safety considerations
screens.narratorSegment: There are a handful of recurring mistakes operators make when advertising routes into BGP. First, forgetting the route exists in inet.0: a network statement silently does nothing if there is no exact-match route. Second, forgetting to set family inet unicast on the BGP group — without it IPv4 exchange will not occur. Third, incorrect or overly-broad export policies can redistribute too many internal routes, leaking internal topology to an ISP or causing routing table growth elsewhere. Another error is incorrect policy logic that never matches, often caused by missing terms or wrong match criteria combined with the implicit deny at the end. To guard against these errors, always test policy behavior with test policy, add precise route-filters or prefix-match terms to limit scope, and verify advertisements with show route advertising-protocol. When working with an ISP, err on the side of more specific filters and explicit accepts rather than broad accepts. Safety-first practices and stepwise verification prevent accidental route leakage and instability on the internet. Module 06 › Chapter 6.5 › Lab: Advertise and Redistribute
Lab steps (R1)
  1. set protocols bgp group EBGP_PEER family inet unicast

# On R2

R2 should receive 172.16.1.0/24 and 10.10.10.1/32 if the static route exists and the export policy is applied.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we'll learn the concrete rules and best practices for injecting routes into BGP on Junos devices. You will learn three primary methods: the network statement for advertising locally originated prefixes, redistribution of routes learned by other protocols through explicit routing policies, and aggregation or summary approaches. We'll also cover a vital operational detail: BGP address families — specifically family inet unicast — and why forgetting it prevents IPv4 routes from being exchanged. Throughout the lesson you'll see exact Junos configuration examples, verification commands to confirm what your router is advertising and receiving, and a short lab scenario to practice advertising a static prefix and redistributing OSPF routes. These skills matter because BGP will not advertise routes by default; explicit, precise configuration decides what your AS tells peers about reachability. By the end you will be able to ensure a prefix exists in the routing table before advertising it, craft export policies that only allow intended routes, and verify the results with show route advertising-protocol and receive-protocol queries. Keep an eye out for common pitfalls like missing family statements or overly-broad redistribution policies that can cause accidental leakage of internal routes.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to identify and configure the common methods Junos uses to advertise routes into BGP, validate that those routes are being sent to a neighbor, and apply safe policies to prevent accidental route leakage. First, you will learn the network statement pattern: how it requires an exact prefix in inet.0 and why operators often add a static discard route to ensure the prefix exists. Second, you will learn how redistribution into BGP is always policy-driven on Junos, allowing you to accept only OSPF, static, or directly connected routes for export. Third, understanding BGP address families is essential; enabling family inet unicast on the BGP group is required to exchange IPv4 routes. Finally, you will learn verification commands like show route advertising-protocol bgp and show route receive-protocol bgp to confirm what is sent and received. Each objective includes a concrete configuration or verification step so you can practice safely and check your results in a lab environment.

This second objectives screen gives practical steps to practice the four goals in a lab safely. For the network statement, create a static route with next-hop discard so the prefix exists in inet.0 before advertising it. Practice the exact-match requirement by trying an incorrect mask and observing no advertisement. For redistribution, build a simple policy-statement that matches protocol ospf and accepts only those prefixes you want to export; test the policy using test policy to confirm behavior before applying it. For address families, explicitly set family inet unicast on the BGP group and observe that without it, your IPv4 advertisements disappear even if the network statement and policy are correct. Finally, practice verification commands: run show route advertising-protocol bgp neighbor-ip and show route receive-protocol bgp neighbor-ip to see sent and received prefixes. Each practice step emphasizes safe testing so you avoid leaking internal prefixes to an ISP during lab exercises.

The network statement is the simplest and most explicit way to tell Junos BGP to advertise a prefix. The key detail is that the network command does not create a route; it only instructs BGP to advertise a prefix if an exact match for that prefix and mask exists in the router's inet.0 table. Practically, this means operators often add a static route with next-hop discard or a connected interface to guarantee the prefix is present. For example, configuring a static route to 172.16.1.0/24 with next-hop discard ensures the prefix is active, then setting network 172.16.1.0/24 under the BGP group causes the router to announce it. A common misconception is that the network statement alone will create reachability; it will not. Another pitfall is using a wrong mask — an exact-match requirement will silently prevent advertisement. Use show route to confirm the prefix is in inet.0 before expecting it to be advertised. The concrete takeaway is: network adds the advertisement only if the router already knows how to reach that prefix. Test this in the lab by adding and removing the static route and observing advertising-protocol output.

Before BGP can advertise a prefix via a network statement, that prefix must be present and active in the inet.0 routing table. There are three common ways to ensure existence: a directly connected interface, a static route, or an aggregate/summary created by static or OSPF configuration. A widely used operational pattern is to add a static route with next-hop discard for summary or non-connected networks. This creates a stable route in inet.0 without pointing traffic into a black hole, and it lets BGP advertise the prefix. Another option is to use an aggregate or summary advertisement if you want to represent many specific prefixes as a single larger prefix — but be careful because summarization changes what you advertise to peers. A practical lab exercise: configure a static discard for 192.168.50.0/24, confirm show route 192.168.50.0/24 returns an active route, then add the network statement. If the route disappears from inet.0 later, BGP will stop advertising it. A common troubleshooting step is to check for more specific routes or route preferences that might suppress the static route from becoming active. Ensure route existence before advertising means guarantee the advertised prefix exists in inet.0 using static, connected, or aggregate routes so bgp will advertise it.. In practical terms, how to make a prefix present in inet.0 so the network statement takes effect. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

BGP is multi-protocol by design: it carries routes for different address families such as IPv4 unicast, IPv6 unicast, and various VPN families. On Junos, each BGP group must explicitly enable the address family you want to exchange. For standard IPv4 routing you must include family inet unicast under the BGP group. If you configure network statements or export policies but forget family inet unicast, the router will not advertise or accept IPv4 unicast routes for that neighbor. This is a common operational mistake and one of the easiest to overlook during peer configuration. In practice, add family inet unicast to every eBGP or iBGP group that will carry IPv4. After enabling, verify peers exchange routes using show route protocol bgp and the advertising/receive-protocol commands. Remember that enabling a family does not itself permit every route — it only allows the exchange of that family subject to your network statements and export policies. A brief misconception check: some operators assume family is global; on Junos it is per-group and must be set per peering relationship. family inet unicast — address-family essentials means family inet unicast must be configured on the bgp group to exchange ipv4 unicast routes; forgetting it prevents ipv4 advertisements.. Redistribution into BGP on Junos is not an implicit action; it is performed by attaching an export policy to a BGP group. Routing policies are the central control point — they let you match routes by protocol, prefix, or route-filter and then accept, reject, or modify attributes before export. A common pattern is to write a policy that matches protocol ospf and accept only those routes you intend to advertise, then attach that policy to the BGP group's export statement. This gives precise control and reduces accidental leaks. For example you can match protocol ospf and then add an additional from route-filter to limit to certain prefixes. A frequent operator error is to write a policy that never matches or to forget that policy-statements have an implicit deny at the end. Always test policies with test policy before applying them to a live BGP session. The architecture pattern here is simple: routing protocols feed the routing table, policies select and manipulate candidates, and BGP exports validated prefixes to peers. The safety and traceability provided by policies are why redistribution on Junos is policy-driven rather than automatic.

When you create an export policy to redistribute OSPF routes into BGP, follow a clear process: define the policy with specific match conditions, test it using test policy, then attach it to the BGP group's export statement. Begin by writing a policy-statement with a term that matches protocol ospf. If you need narrower control, add a from route-filter clause for the desired prefixes. After you write the policy, use show policy policy-statement detail to inspect its terms, and use test policy to simulate how the policy would act on a sample route. Testing prevents surprises and the common error of implicit deny. Once verified, apply the policy to the BGP group with set protocols bgp group export. After applying, verify with show route advertising-protocol bgp to see the actual exported prefixes. These are the essential terms to keep in mind when advertising routes into BGP on Junos. First, the network statement advertises a specified prefix only when that exact prefix exists in the local routing table. Second, redistribution is the controlled process of injecting routes learned by other protocols into BGP; on Junos this is always driven by routing policies. Third, a routing policy is a set of match and action rules that decide which routes are imported, exported, or modified by a protocol. Keep these short definitions in your mental toolbox as you configure and verify BGP advertisements.
